style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Studies, and general knowledge.
Can I mention studies in the essay? Can I make them up? Should I? Let's see.
So what's the goal when I cite a study in an argument paragraph? I'm trying to prove my argument. To make the explanation stronger.
So it's really another kind of support. We learned support by example, and by comparison. So maybe also... support by a study?
What's the problem?
In the exam, we don't really have studies. We can't stop and search online.
So either you happen to know a real study. Or you're tempted to make one up.
And if you know a real one... well, maybe there's another study that shows exactly the opposite. One you don't know about.
Making up a study? Here the answer is short. And it comes from the official guide itself.
The guide tells you to avoid illogical, incorrect or fabricated information.
A made-up study is fabricated information. So is a made-up percentage. A made-up expert. A made-up city where it supposedly worked.
So that question is closed. We don't make things up. Ever.
And as you'll see now, even a real study doesn't help you the way you'd think.
First, a difference in wording.
'Studies have shown that'. That's general. I'm not talking about a specific study.
'A recent study conducted in some city found that crime dropped by some percentage.' Now that's describing a specific study. With a year, a country, a number.
The rater isn't going to stop and look it up. And that's exactly the trap. It sounds precise, and if you made it up, it's exactly what the guide means by fabricated information.
But here's the part most students don't realize.
Say you mention a study: in streets with face-recognition cameras, crime went down. Fine. What does the rater want next? Explain it.
Why did crime go down there? What happened? Now you have to explain the result, with logic.
So, in other words, you're back to development. Explaining the mechanism.
Wait. The study was supposed to make my explanation stronger. But now I have to explain the study? It's chicken and egg.
So citing a study doesn't make the argument stronger. It's like making another claim. One that itself needs to be developed and supported.
The downsides. It adds no strength, because you have to explain it anyway. It wastes time, and it might count as padding.
It looks like you're running away from explaining. Like, this writer can't explain, so they cite. And raters come from academia, where 'a study showed' with no source is a no-no.
And the rater might know the field. If it's wrong, or made up, it's fabricated information. And the guide says clearly to avoid that.
And the upsides? None. So from today, you don't cite specific studies anymore.
So what can you say? General knowledge that's well established.
There are things everyone knows were proven. Smoking harms health. Regular exercise is good for health.
That's fine to use. It's a fact today, and you're not making anything up.
But I would never write: studies have shown that face-recognition cameras cut crime by fifty percent. That's my opinion, dressed up as research. With a made-up number.
So the rule is: if you're not sure it's true, it doesn't go in.
And even for real, well-known facts, I like to use a little trick.
Instead of 'studies have shown', I write: 'it is now well known that'.
What does 'it is now well known' mean? Once, people didn't know it. Today they do. How? Because studies were done. So I'm saying the same thing, just without the word 'studies'.
For facts you're sure of: it is now well known that. It is generally accepted that.
And for your own reasoning, which is most of the essay: it is reasonable to expect that. This is likely to, since. In many cases.
That's honest phrasing. A known fact, said as a fact. Your prediction, said as a prediction. And the explanation does the work.
Bottom line. No specific studies. Nothing made up. Well-known true facts, yes, with 'it is now well known'. And your own claims: explain them, and phrase them honestly.
